One born in the sign of Aquarius (Ghaṭaja) is devoted to the wives of others, to wealth, and to sinful acts; he experiences both loss and gain, is fond of flowers and ointments, and is capable of enduring long journeys.

(Troṭaka) In the final zodiac sign (Pisces), one who enjoys water and the wealth of others, is deeply attached to his wife and clothing, possesses a symmetrical and beautiful body, a prominent nose, and large limbs;
he overcomes his rivals, is ruled by women, has lovely eyes, is a treasury of luster, an enjoyer of wealth, and is wise. (Mālinī)

If the Moon is in a strong sign and its lord is endowed with its own strength, it bestows the aforementioned digits in their entirety; others are to be considered differently from this, like the moon [in other circumstances]. (Bhramaravilasita) E17: The Nature of Signs.

When the Sun is in Taurus, one becomes famous, travels in the four directions, possesses little wealth, is engaged in religious rites, and carries weapons; in the portion of Virgo, one lives by selling cattle, clothing, and perfumes, is skilled with women, and is devoted to cows, barley, and the like. (In Aries: One possesses learning, astrology, and wealth. When the Sun is situated in Gemini, one is fierce, lacks horses, performs the work of others, and is joined with the hardships of laborious paths. (In Cancer: [One is] afflicted by the distress of laborious paths.

If [the Moon] is situated in Leo, the man is devoted to forests, mountains, and herds of cattle, endowed with valor, yet ignorant. If it is in Virgo, he is endowed with knowledge of writing, scripts, poetry, and mathematics, and possesses a feminine form. (Śārṅgadharapaddhati 10.23) One born when the Moon is in Libra is a vintner, devoted to travel, a goldsmith, base, cruel, impetuous, and one who has acquired wealth through service. If it is in Scorpio, he is a master of weapons. (Śārṅgadharapaddhati 10.24) When the Moon has gone to Sagittarius, he is honored by the virtuous and wealthy. In Capricorn, he is sharp, a physician, a craftsman, base, ignorant, a wicked womanizer, possessing little wealth, and dependent on the fortune of others. (Śārṅgadharapaddhati 10.25)

In the division resembling the body of a man or a star, when conjoined with the Moon or the Sun, one should predict the following: [If the Moon is there,] a low-born man, deprived of children and fortune, possessing wealth from water-born merchandise, and separated from his wife at the end of the rainy season. [If Mars is there,] one should predict:

honored by the king, wandering, a commander of an army, a wealthy merchant, with an injured body, and many territories acquired through theft. (Vṛttamālā) In its own house, Mars [produces these results].
One born under Śatabhiṣaj (the White Star) produces sons who conquer young women, are treacherous toward friends, addicted to the wives of others, deceitful, well-dressed, cowardly, and impudent.
(Troṭaka) Under Baudha (Punarvasu), one has many sons but lacks self-control; he is unfriendly yet grateful, skilled in the art of amorous combat, miserly, fearless, and needy.
Under Cāndra (Mṛgaśiras), one is wealthy, acquires property by means of water transport, and is wise. Under Bhūmitanaya (Bṛhaspati/Maghā), one is physically deformed and wicked. (Va.ti)

When Mars is situated in Aquarius (Kumbha), the minister of a lord of men is penniless, enduring afflictions, wandering in the depths of the forest, having few wives and sons, possessing few enemies, renowned, fearless, and having few offspring;

he is afflicted by suffering, destitute, a wanderer, devoted to falsehood, and harsh. When Mars has gone to Capricorn (Mṛga), he possesses abundant wealth and sons, or else becomes a king or equal to one.
In the sign of Mars (Capricorn), those devoted to gambling, debt, drinking, atheism, theft, poverty, wicked women, deceit, and untruthfulness [are found].
In the sub-period of Venus, one gains teachers, many sons, a wife, and wealth; one is devoted to sacrifices and is liberal and intent on service to elders.
In the sub-period of Mercury (Va-ti), one is boastful, skilled in the sciences and arts, pleasant of speech, and devoted to pleasure.
In the sub-period of the Moon joined with the constellation Mṛgaśiras, one acquires property through water, becomes an enemy to one's own kin, and is fond of comfort.

When Mercury is in the sign of the Sun (Leo), the native is hated by women, lacks wealth and happiness, has no children, is a wanderer, ignorant, lustful after women, and suffers humiliation from his own kin.

When it is in the sixth sign (Virgo), he is generous, wise, possessed of many virtues, happy, patient, skilled in reasoning, and free from fear. When Mercury is in the asterism of Saturn (Pūrvaphalgunī), he performs the work of others, lacks skill in his own craft, is burdened with debt, and is a forced laborer.

In the ninth house, a man is honored by kings, possesses the speech of learned and trustworthy men, and has conquered his servants and mastered the final arts. In the tenth house, he leads an army, possesses abundant wealth, wives, and sons, is charitable, has good servants, is patient, and is endowed with splendor, a wife, and virtues; such a man is renowned when Jupiter is in the sign of Mars. In the eleventh house, he is well-proportioned in body, possesses wealth, purpose, friends, and sons, is generous, and is beloved when Venus is there. In the twelfth house, under Mercury, he has many attendants, sons, and friends, is endowed with ministerial office, and is happy.

In Leo, one endowed with the Moon will possess jewels, sons, one's own wife, wealth, wisdom, and happiness; he will be a leader of an army, as has been declared for the period of Jupiter when it is in the lunar sign of Leo.

In its own asterism, [Mars] makes a man a regional ruler, a minister of a king, a commander-in-chief, or wealthy; in Aquarius, its results are like those in Cancer. In Capricorn, it is debilitated, resulting in little wealth and unhappiness.
(Śārdūlavikrīḍita) In the asterism of Mars, one is devoted to the wives of others, has his wealth stolen through their entreaties, and is a defiler of his family.
In its own [sign], Venus makes one strong in power and intellect, wealthy, honored by kings, a lord over his own people, famous, and fearless. (Puṣpitāgrā)
When Saturn has reached the sixth sign from Gemini, one becomes a performer of royal duties, wealthy, and skilled in the arts; yet his actions are exceedingly base.
When Saturn reaches the asterism of the worshipful enemy of the gods (Pūrvaphalgunī), he is fortunate but conquered by women, devoted to unchaste ladies.

If it is in the asterism of Hari (Śravaṇā), he has two wives, is desirous of wealth, timid, and possesses intense passion and grief; he acquires wealth through women, possesses excellent young wives, but has dull-witted sons.
When Jupiter is in Pisces along with a horse (the Sun), one is honored for his virtues; he is learned, wealthy, honored by kings, and exceedingly handsome.
(Śikhariṇī meter) In Capricorn, one is foolish, wandering, deceitful, and friendless; in Aries, however, he suffers imprisonment and death, being fickle and merciless.
He is shameless, possesses sons for the sake of pleasure, and is prone to stumbling in writing. In Sagittarius, he becomes a chief protector and a principal leader. (Vaṃśastha meter)

When Venus is in Taurus, one is avoided by women, lacks great wealth, has many wives, and is famous; if it is in its own exaltation, he is honored by his clan, city, army, and village, and is wealthy. In Cancer, he is without horses, has defective teeth, is motherless, childless, and ignorant. In Leo, he is ignoble, unhappy, sonless, and performs menial labor under Saturn. (In Mandākrāntā meter: When Saturn enters the domicile of Jupiter, a man becomes well-disposed, trusted, possesses good sons, wife, and wealth, and becomes a leader of cities, armies, and villages.

(Śārṅgadharapaddhati) The Moon causes auspicious results when it occupies the lord of the ascendant (horā), its own sign (īśa), or half of its own asterism (ṛkṣa-dala), and is aspected by benefics. It is likewise praised when situated in the third part (try-aṃśa) of that sign and aspected by the lords of those divisions, or by planets occupying friendly houses. Whatever result has been declared for the aspect on each zodiac sign (rāśi), that same result is traditionally held to apply to the twelve parts (dvādaśāṃśa). When the Sun is in the house of the Moon (Cancer), one is blind, destitute, and eyeless like a bubble; in the house of the Sun (Leo), one possesses abundant wealth but has his riches seized by the king; in the second house (Virgo), one is crooked and diseased. (Mandākrāntā) In the third house (Libra), the Sun brings intelligence and valor; in the fourth house (Scorpio), one is turned away from others and afflicted in honor. In the trines (Sagittarius and Pisces), one is childless and devoid of wealth; when gone to the enemy sign (Aries), one is powerful and conquers enemies. (Aupacchandasika)

When the Moon has gone to the seventh house, one suffers humiliation from women; when it is in the eighth, one has few children and impaired vision; in the ninth, one enjoys children, wealth, and happiness; in the tenth, one possesses happiness and valor; in the eleventh, one is possessed of abundant wealth; but in the twelfth, one is fallen. At the rising of the Moon (the birth), if it is situated in its own asterism or its exaltation, one is mute, insane, dull-witted, blind, deficient, deaf, or a servant; if it is in the second house, one is wealthy, has many sons, and is self-possessed with a large family.

When the Moon is in the second house, one is violent, finds happiness through brothers, has sons, and is endowed with the qualities of that house; it brings many enemies, a delicate body, moderate digestive fire, passion, sharpness, and laziness in the sixth house. (Śāravi) In the seventh house, one is envious, intensely intoxicated, highly intelligent, afflicted by disease, and in the eighth house, afflicted by illness. When the Moon is situated in the ninth house, one partakes in good fortune, children, friends, kinsmen, and wealth. (Śāravi) In the tenth house, one attains success and is endowed with righteousness, wealth, intellect, and valor. In the eleventh house, one is famous and endowed with the virtues of that house; in the twelfth house, one is mean and deficient in limbs. (Śāravi)
If Mars is in the ascendant, the body is wounded; in the second house, one has poor food; in the ninth house, one is sinful; and in other positions, he is like the sun.
When Mercury is there, one is learned, wealthy, a wicked scholar, a minister, free from enemies, a knower of dharma, and renowned for his virtues—just like the sun.
[In the case of Jupiter: He is learned, eloquent, miserly, happy, intelligent, an enemy, and superior to his father.
When Jupiter is in the ascendant, one is base; in the second house, an ascetic; in the third, wealthy; in the fourth, one with gains; and in the fifth, a villain.
(Indravajrā) When Venus is in the ascendant, one is skilled in love and happy; in the seventh house, prone to quarrels with loved ones yet desiring sexual union;
in the fifth house, happy; and in the twelfth house, like a teacher, one is wealthy in another's home. (Citratā)

When Saturn is in the ascendant, the person is one whose purpose remains unseen, is diseased, under the sway of passion, extremely filthy, and afflicted by pain in childhood; such is the speech of the indolent. However, if Jupiter is situated in its own asterism or its exaltation, he is said to be like a king, a ruler of villages and cities, highly learned, with beautiful limbs, and equal to the sun in brilliance. (Śikhariṇī meter) One should consider the results of planets situated in the houses of friends, enemies, others, or their own asterisms and exaltations, according to the houses of the body, the ascendant, and so forth.

A true sage declares that [planets] situated in the eleventh, second, third, and fourth houses produce accumulation, while those in malefic houses produce its opposite; however, this is reversed for planets in the twelfth, sixth, and eighth houses.
(Mālinī) [The results of a planet's position] are auspicious when it is in its exaltation, trine, own house, friend's house, enemy's house, depression, or the house of the Sun;
these results are respectively full, three-quarters, half, one-quarter, small, and nil. (Anuṣṭubh) E20

Through the increase of one's own sign, there is the yoga of the physical basis (*āśrayayoga*): [one becomes] a chief of a family, equal to a family, a leader, a kinsman, venerable, wealthy, happy, an enjoyer of pleasures, or a king.

Through the increase of a friendly sign, [one becomes] one who prospers through the wealth of others, a friend, a supporter of one's own kin, a leader of a guild (*gaṇapa*), a commander of forces, or a king. (Puṣpitāgrā meter)
Even a single planet, when exalted and aspected by a friend, produces a king endowed with abundant wealth; through the conjunction with a friend, such results are perfected.

However, when situated in the houses of enemies, debilitated signs, or inimical planets, one becomes destitute, averse to fortune, deluded, afflicted by disease, tormented by imprisonment, and beset by execution and sin.
Satya says that Aquarius is not a favorable ascendant, while the Yavanas say this is not so because of the division of the lunar mansions.
Viṣṇugupta [states]: "There is no such division of degrees for a sign as there is for a house; otherwise, it would lead to an over-extension.

When the malefics have gone to their own or similar signs, one born in the *horā* of the lord of the day becomes famous, possessed of great exertion, strength, and wealth, and endowed with intense luster.
When the benefics are in even signs, one born in the *horā* of the Moon is endowed with gentleness, beauty, happiness, good fortune, intelligence, and sweet speech.

In those very same hours, men are to be known as superior when the planets are situated in their own or friendly signs; they are mediocre when situated in the opposite signs; and when situated in signs contrary to the hour, mortals become devoid of the aforementioned qualities. (Indravajrā) When the Moon is in its own or friendly Navāṃśa or Trikoṇa, it bestows auspicious form and qualities; when it is in another [sign], it produces the qualities of the lord of that [sign].

In the first quarter (navāṃśa), one becomes a rogue, a snake, one who rises with weapons, a four-legged creature, or a bird; one who is sharp, excessively violent, devoted to violating the teacher’s bed, and a wanderer.

(Va-ti) In the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth quarters respectively, one becomes a thief, an enjoyer, a learned man, a wealthy person, a king, a eunuch, a hero, a laborer, a servant, a sinner, a violent person, and fearless—these being the results for these [planets] in their respective twelve parts, like the signs of the zodiac. (Śālinī)
When Mars is in its own division (svabhāga), one is accompanied by a wife, possesses strength, ornaments, and courage, and is endowed with brilliance and great daring.
When in the division of the Son of the Sun (Sauri), one is diseased, has a deceased wife, is harsh, takes another's wife, is miserable, yet possessed of attendants, and is filthy.

(Va-ti) When Jupiter is in its own portion (svāṃśa), one is endowed with wealth, fame, happiness, and intelligence; he is brilliant, venerable, free from disease, industrious, and possesses enjoyments.
In the case of Mercury (Śaśija), those endowed with intelligence, arts, eloquence, poetry, debate, craftsmanship, the meaning of the scriptures, and daring are highly esteemed.
(Va-ti) In its own thirtieth degree, one possesses many sons, happiness, health, fortune, wealth, and beauty; under Venus (Śukra), one is sharp, has a very graceful body, and well-developed senses.

In the degrees beginning with Mars (Āra-pūrva-aṃśaka) joined by the Sun, Moon, and Mercury, there are eight types of men: heroic, stubborn, treacherous killers, rich in good qualities, happy, and handsome-limbed. (Mandākrāntā) E21

Those planets situated in their own, exaltation, Mūlatrikoṇa, or Kaṇṭaka houses, as many as are occupied therein, are all mutual Karakas; however, among them, those situated in the tenth house (Karma-bhāva) are especially so. (In Vaitālīya meter)
When the Moon has entered the rising sign of Cancer, Mars, Saturn, the Sun, and Jupiter are said to be its respective significators (kārakas), each occupying its own exaltation;
likewise, every planet situated in the ascendant, the tenth, or the fourth house is a significator for one another.
Furthermore, if a planet occupies its own trine or exaltation while being in the seventh house from another, it acts as a mutual cause for that other planet.

One endowed with those [auspicious] qualities is considered a *suhṛt* (friend), and he is also known as a *kāraka* (agent). (Anuṣṭubh) A birth in an excellent division (*varga*), in a *veśi* position, or in a good house;
and when the planets known as *kārakas* occupy non-vacant *kendras*: (Anuṣṭubh)

Jupiter, the lord of the birth sign, and the lord of the ascendant, when situated in angles during the middle of their periods, bestow happiness; however, when they occupy signs that rise from the back, both sides, or the front, they grant results at the end, the middle, and the beginning [of their periods] respectively. (In Vaitālīya meter) At the time of entry, the Sun and Mars [grant results] in the first part, while Jupiter and Venus, having reached the middle of the house, [grant results] in the middle.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) and the Moon, situated in the *vinirgama* [the eighth house], do not grant results; however, the son of the Moon (Mercury) grants results at all times.

(Puṣpitāgrā meter) If, from an unfavorable ascendant, the houses of the son and wife are occupied by benefics or their lords, or are aspected by the Moon, then indeed there is prosperity for those two; otherwise, the opposite should be understood to occur.

Pāṭhā: When the Sun has not yet risen and Saturn is situated in Pisces, he destroys the wife; when situated in the house of children, he brings about the death of the son; and the son of the Earth (Mars) bestows a son.

Śārdūlavikrīḍita: When Venus is situated in a square from fierce planets, or when Mercury is situated between two fierce planets, and is neither conjoined with nor aspected by gentle planets, there is the death of the wife caused by fire, falling [from a height], or a noose.
They say that birth occurs with a wife when the Moon and the Sun are situated in the twelfth and sixth houses from the ascendant, and one of them is conjoined with a malefic planet.
Or, they declare that one born when Venus and the Sun are situated in the seventh house, or in the ninth and fifth houses respectively, is born without a wife.

(Vṛtta-taraṅgiṇī) If Venus is in a trine or the ascendant at the time of birth, or at the junction of its setting and the zodiacal sign, the man is the husband of a barren woman, provided the sign of the Moon is not joined with a benefic planet.
When malefic planets are situated in the twelfth, seventh, or first houses, and the Moon is waning while positioned in the fifth, seventh, first, or fifth house from the ascendant;
(Mālinī meter) If Venus or Mars is in its own division, situated in the seventh house, and aspected by the Moon—provided these two are not aspected by the Moon—the man will be unfaithful to his wife.

If Venus and the Moon are in the seventh house, the man will be without a wife or without sons; however, if the Sun and Moon aspect the seventh house, the husband and wife will both be advanced in years. (Hariṇī meter)

One who cuts the lineage [is born] when the Moon, Venus, Jupiter, and malefics occupy the tenth house; one becomes an artisan when Mercury is in its own third-part (tri-aṃśa), conjoined with [another planet], and aspected by Saturn situated in a quadrant. One born of a slave woman occurs when Jupiter is in the twelfth house in a portion belonging to Saturn. One is base-born when the Sun and Moon are in the seventh house, aspected by Saturn. When Venus and Mars are aspected by malefics or situated in the seventh house, and the Moon is in Cancer or Scorpio, conjoined with malefics, there is disease of the private parts.

If two malefic planets are situated in the second and seventh houses from the ascendant, and the Sun is at its rising while the Moon is at its setting, or if the Moon is in the tenth house and Mars is heliacally set, and Saturn is in the ninth house, there is distress.
(Śārṅgadhara-paddhati) When the Moon is between two malefics and the Sun is in Capricorn, one suffers from asthma, consumption, splenic disorders, abscesses, or abdominal tumors.
If the Sun and Moon occupy each other’s signs and degrees, or if they are both in the same sign in their respective signs, one becomes emaciated. (Vṛtta-taraṅgiṇī)

One becomes afflicted with leprosy if Saturn is situated in the middle of Aśvinī, Citrā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, or Revatī, or if it is aspected by Mars or Mars' planet (Mars).

Alternatively, one is a leper if the Sun, Moon, Mars, or Saturn are situated in the third, fifth, ninth, or twelfth house from the ascendant, or if they are in Scorpio, Cancer, Taurus, or Capricorn, and are either conjoined with or aspected by malefic planets.
(Va-ti) If the Sun, Moon, Mars, and Saturn are situated in the eighth, sixth, second, or twelfth house respectively...
Due to the influence of powerful planetary afflictions, they cause blindness in men.

(Vaitālīya) If [the lords of] the ninth, eleventh, third, and fifth houses are joined with malefics, are not aspected by benefics, and are necessarily situated in the seventh house, they cause deafness and deformities of the teeth. (Vaitālīya)
When the moon rises, that demon of misfortune is in the third and ninth houses;

when the sun rises within the orb of an eclipse, he is deprived of sight. When Mars is conjoined with Rāhu in the seventh house or the ascendant, one suffers from madness; likewise, when Jupiter is situated in the seventh house and Mars is placed in the ascendant.

Similarly, when the son of the Sun (Saturn) has risen, the son of the Earth (Mars) is in the seventh house, the son of Dharma (Jupiter) is in the fifth house, the son of the Thousand-Rayed One (Venus) is born, and the Moon is waning in its period of expenditure—(Śārṅgadharapaddhati 107).

When the signs and degrees occupied by the Sun, the Moon, and Jupiter are situated in their respective debilitation or exaltation signs, or in the portions of their enemies, those born from these [planets] being weak, middling, or strong respectively should be known as slaves by servitude, purchase, or birth. (Varṣatantra 4.26)

If the Sun rises in Aries or Taurus and is aspected by malefic planets, the man will have deformed teeth; if the Ascendant is in Scorpio or Taurus and situated in an inauspicious *bhava*, he will be bald; if the Sun is in the ninth or fifth house and aspected by malefics, his eyes will be weak; if Saturn is there, he suffers from many diseases; and if Mars is there, the man becomes physically impaired. When malefic planets occupy the twelfth, fifth, second, and ninth houses, one must calculate the loss of one's home and honor.
Likewise, when the signs of the arms, the multitude of clubs, and the noose are aspected by strong malefics, it is similar.

(Puṣpitāgrā) When the Moon has entered the sign of Saturn, and that [Saturn] has gone to the aspect of Venus or is surrounded by a halo, one afflicted by epilepsy speaks like a man and suffers from consumption.

(Hariṇī) When the Sun, Yama (Saturn), and Mars occupy the sky (the tenth house) without being aspected by benefics, the men previously mentioned—whether superior, inferior, or middling—become servants. (Hariṇī) E23
Whatever results are appropriate for men in the *strījātaka* (astrology of women), one should declare all of those for women as well, or rather, they should be applied to their husbands.

For them, however, the death of the husband occurs when [the Moon] is in the eighth house (*nidhana*); physical beauty when it is in the ascendant (*lagna*) or the Moon-sign; and good fortune, as well as the husband, when it is in the seventh house (*astamaya*). (Vṛtta-taraṅgiṇī)
When the Ascendant and the Moon are in even signs and aspected by benefics, the woman is naturally disposed, endowed with good character and ornaments;

when they are in odd signs, she possesses a human form and disposition. If they are conjoined with or aspected by malefics, she is devoid of virtues. (Vṛtta-taraṅgiṇī) A maiden who is [thus] wicked becomes a slave in this world; one who is virtuous yet deceitful is joined with misconduct.
In the divisions (aṃśakas) of the signs ruled by Mars, the Moon, Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus respectively, the woman born under Saturn will be wicked;
under Rahu, she will be a remarried woman; under Jupiter, virtuous and skilled in the arts; and under Venus, famous for her virtues. Under Mars, she will be deceitful;
under Mercury, like a eunuch; under Ketu, chaste; and under the Moon, rich in virtues yet possessed of scattered desires.

In the Indu-bha (Moon-sign), she is a self-willed slayer of her husband, possessing many virtues, and skilled in the arts, yet unchaste. In the Arka-bha (Sun-sign), she follows the conduct of men, is unfaithful, and is a king’s wife who acts like a man and goes to forbidden men. With the Jiva-bha (Jupiter-sign), she has few virtues and little passion, yet is highly virtuous, wise, and chaste. In the Arki-bha (Saturn-sign), she is a servant, delights in low men, and though devoted to her husband, is wicked; these results are determined by their respective portions (aṃśakas). (Śā.vi. This result is derived from the thirty degrees (triṃśāṃśaka) joined with the Moon and the Ascendant.

One should reflect upon what has been stated regarding those two [the Moon and Venus] by means of an analysis of their strength and weakness. (Anuṣṭubh) If Venus is situated in the seventh house from the Ascendant, or if it is conjoined with the Moon, or if its own portion is in the sign of Aquarius, then a person—though appearing in human form—is brought to peace by women who are like the fire of the poison of female passion. (Prahārṣiṇī)

If the seventh house is empty, occupied by a base person (kāpuruṣa), or devoid of strength, and is aspected by a benefic planet, the woman is a coward (klība). If Mercury and Saturn are in the seventh house, which is a movable sign (cara-gṛha), she is constantly away from home.

If the Sun and Mars abandon the seventh house, she becomes a widow in her youth; if a malefic aspects it while the daughter remains in that same seventh sign, she reaches old age [as a widow]. (Śāravi) If the seventh house is occupied by planets belonging to Agni (Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn), she becomes a widow; if it is mixed with both types, she becomes a remarried woman (punarbhū). If a malefic planet with diminished strength is set (astamita) and aspected by a benefic, she is abandoned by her own husband.

If Venus and Mars occupy each other’s signs and are attached to another woman, or if they are with the Moon in the seventh house, then [the wife] belongs to the husband only with his permission. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita) If Saturn or Mars is in the ascendant at the time of birth, and Venus is with the Moon and aspected by malefic planets, she is an unchaste woman; if Mars is in its sign of debilitation and Saturn is in its Navamsha, she is born from disease; but if it is in the Navamsha of a benefic planet, she has beautiful hips and is beloved. (Śālinī)
If the Sun is in the *nakṣatra* or *aṃśaka* of Mars, the husband will be old, foolish, and lustful toward women; if in that of the Earth (Mars), he will be wrathful.
If in that of Venus, he will be exceedingly handsome and endowed with great good fortune; if in that of Mercury, he will be learned, a master, and discerning of skill.
(In the *mālinī* meter: Under the Moon, he is subject to the power of passion and gentle; under Jupiter, the son of the Thirty-three Gods, he is virtuous and has conquered his senses.
If the Sun is situated in its house of setting or in its own *aṃśaka*, she performs very tender acts of love and possesses valor.

(Puṣpitāgrā meter) If the Moon is in the ascendant with Venus, she is full of jealousy yet devoted to pleasure; if it is with Mercury and the Moon, she is skilled in the arts, happy, and rich in virtues.

If both Venus and Mercury are there, she is radiant, fortunate, and knowledgeable in the arts; if all three are in benefic positions, she possesses manifold wealth, happiness, and virtues. (Vaṃśastha meter)

If a malefic planet is in the eighth house, widowhood is indicated; if it is situated in the lord of the eighth house's *aṃśa* (navāṃśa), it is predicted for her at an age equal to that [of the planet]. If the planets are in their own or exaltation signs, she dies by her own hand. If the Sun is there, she has no children; if Venus, she has few sons; and if the Moon, she has daughters. (Va-ti) If Saturn possesses middling strength, while the Moon, Venus, and Mercury are devoid of strength, and the remaining planets are endowed with full vigor, she will be a woman of harsh speech if the rising sign is an odd-numbered one (*oja-rāśi*).

When Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and Mercury are strong, and the sign on the eastern horizon (the ascendant) is even, there arises on earth a woman renowned for her mastery of many scriptures, even one who speaks upon the Brahman.
(Śārdūlavikrīḍita) Without doubt, when a malefic planet is in the seventh house, a young woman enters into a life of renunciation equal to that of a planet situated in the ninth house;
this entire matter should be considered during marriage, the ceremony of choosing a bridegroom, the time of giving her away, and even in deliberation. (Praharṣiṇī) E24

In the eighth house, death occurs through the sight of the abode of death (the cremation ground) by those who are powerful; it arises from the agitation of the bodily elements (dhātus) associated with that [planet], or from many births resulting from injuries to the limbs caused by that [planet]. It is also caused by fire, water, weapons, fever, disease, thirst, and hunger. In the case of the Sun and other planets situated in the *cara* and other [movements] at the time of death (*nidhana*), death occurs while traveling on a journey or in foreign lands. (Śāravi)

If the Sun and Mars are struck by a mountain peak while situated in the tenth or fourth house, death occurs; or if Saturn, the Moon, and Mars are situated in the seventh, eighth, or eleventh house, death occurs in a well. If the Sun and Moon are in Virgo, aspected by malefic planets, and both are heliacally risen, then the person is drowned in water. (Śārṅgadharīya) If Saturn is in Cancer, death is caused by dropsy; if the Moon is in Capricorn, death arises from weapons or fire; and if the Moon is situated between two malefics in the sign of Mars, [death follows].

When the Moon is situated in Virgo, afflicted by blood, fever, and consumption, and likewise in the solar asterism (Pūrvaphalgunī), and similarly when the cold-rayed one (the Moon) is in the asterisms of Rohiṇī and Kṛttikā, [death occurs] through ropes and fire.

(Śārṅgadharapaddhati) If the fifth and ninth houses from those two malefics are aspected by a benefic planet, and if the decans (dreṣkāṇas) are occupied by malefics with nooses, snakes, and shackles, there is imprisonment.

Know that if the Moon, conjoined with a malefic, is in its setting sign (in the seventh house), and the Sun is in Aries while the Ascendant is occupied by Saturn, death caused by a woman shall occur in the home. (Śārṅgadharapaddhati)

If the son of the Earth (Mars) is in the tenth house, or the Sun is in the tenth or the seventh house, and the Moon is simultaneously afflicted by malefic planets occupying the trines and other such positions, the body is pierced by sharp pain.

When the Sun is situated in the fourth house and Mars is in the tenth house, aspected by the waning Moon, one goes to death struck by a wooden staff, provided it is also aspected by Saturn. (Śārṅgadharapaddhati) When the eighth, first, third, fourth, and second houses are occupied by Mars, the waning Moon, Rahu, the Sun, and Jupiter respectively, one's body is struck by a club.
When those same planets are situated in the tenth, ninth, ascendant, and fifth houses, the end comes through smoke, fire, imprisonment, and the crushing of the body. (Vṛttatārāvalī)
When Mars, the Sun, and Saturn are conjoined with the *bandhu* (twelfth), *asta* (seventh), and *karma* (tenth) houses, death occurs due to weapons, fire, or the wrath of a king.
When Saturn, the Moon, and Mars are situated in their own signs, their own houses of happiness, or their own *āspada* (exaltation), bodily injury caused by wounds or worms should be known [to occur].

If the Sun is in the tenth house and Mars has gone to the netherworld (the fourth house), death results from falling from a vehicle; if Mars is at its setting (in the seventh house) and is joined by Saturn and the Moon, death results from being crushed by a machine.
When Saturn is situated in Libra, Aries, or Capricorn along with Mars, the Sun, and the Moon, or when the Moon, the Sun, and Mars have fallen from the sky [the tenth house] to the seventh house;

(Śārdūlavikrīḍita) And when the waning Moon is aspected by a strong retrograde planet while Saturn is placed in the eighth house, death shall occur due to suffering from a disease arising in the private parts, caused by worms, weapons, or burns. (Vaitālīya)
If Saturn is in Aśleṣā, Mars is in Mūlā, Rāhu is in the eighth house, Venus is waning and has gone to Rasātala, and the Moon is within the sign of Sagittarius;

and if the Sun, Mars, Saturn, and the Moon occupy the ascendant, the fifth, the eighth, and the tenth houses respectively, then death occurs due to the fall of a mountain peak, a thunderbolt, or a wall.
Thus, the twenty-second Dreṣkāṇa has been described by the learned as the cause of death.
Or rather, its lord, Bhava, bestows liberation through his own qualities.
(Vaitālīya) This should be determined from the conjunctions, aspects, and so forth, when the hour, the ninth-part, and the sub-period are situated in their own respective houses.
However, at the time of death, delusion is equal to the rising sign; it is doubled if aspected by its own lord, and tripled if aspected by benefics. (Vaitālīya)
"By means of fire and water, through the processes of burning, moistening with ash, and drying, they reach their end within the dwellings of the serpent-hosts;
thus should one contemplate the transformation of the corpse as described in the extensive scriptures, considering its subsequent states of transition and so forth.
(Mālinī meter) The Guru, the Moon, and Venus [lead to] gods; the Sun and Mars [to] ancestors; and Mercury and Saturn [to] animals and those in hell.
From the lord of the three signs presided over by the strength of the Sun and Moon, the planets are classified as superior, equal, or inferior according to their exaltation or depression.

(Mālinī) Furthermore, if Jupiter is situated in the sixth, eighth, or third house from the ascendant, or in the seventh house, or occupies an enemy sign, a quadrant, or a trine, yet is placed in its own or its exaltation sign;
and if it rises in the last house (the twelfth) or in a benefic portion, there is liberation provided that the remaining planets are devoid of strength. (Mālinī) E25
In the case of a lost horoscope, when the time of conception and birth is unknown, one should declare the birth from the ascendant (lagna) for one who asks about it.
One should find the birth in the eastern or western half of the house, depending on whether the sun is in the northern or southern course.
Having determined Jupiter’s positions in the ascendant and its trines according to their respective triplicities, one should calculate the years by inferring from the age.

When the Sun is in the ascendant, it is said to be summer; by the remaining [signs], the other seasons are determined according to the Sun’s movement. The Moon, Mercury, and Jupiter are to be rotated [through the signs] in the reverse order during the solstices when Venus, Mars, and Saturn are present.
In the first third-part (dreṣkāṇa), the first month [is determined], and the lunar day (tithi) is to be calculated by proportion.
Here too, the masters of horā, O best of the twice-born, declare the lunar day to be equal to the degrees of the sun.
In those [periods] designated as night and day, the times (velā) are to be calculated respectively by the reverse and birth portions.

Some call the month known as Śuklānta that which is occupied by the moon (the hare-marked one) during its ninth degree; or it is declared to be when [the Moon] possesses excellent strength in the ascendant or a trine, or through [the occurrence of] limb-injury and so forth. One should state the birth sign to be at as many degrees from the ascendant as the cool-rayed moon has traversed from the Moon itself.
When Pisces is rising, a pair of fish is indicated; it should be considered through the food consumed, the appearance, and the sounds [heard].

(Indravajrā) The ascendant is like the hour-angle (horā) and the ninth-part (navāṃśa); from the ascendant, one should state the ascendant of the querent at birth to be as many signs away as the Sun is from the decan (dṛkāṇa). Thus says the scripture. (Indravajrā)
If the Moon is in the ascendant at birth or possesses strength, the remainder of the calculation—obtained by multiplying the shadow in finger-breadths—is declared as follows:

it indicates whether one is seated, asleep, risen, or standing; and its placement in the ascendant is said to grant happiness through one's wife and authority. (Indravajrā meter) The signs of Taurus, Leo, Aries, Libra, Virgo, and Capricorn are to be multiplied by ten, eight, seven, and five respectively; the remaining signs are multiplied by their own numerical values.

The Sun, Mars, Saturn, and Rāhu follow the rule of the first [sign], while the remaining planets follow the rule of the Moon. This fixed rule applies to the signs; and by means of the planetary conjunctions, their *vargaṇā* (grouping) should be performed.
(Śāravi) Having added the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) corresponding to the remainder left after dividing seven times the product by twenty-seven, or having subtracted nine from it, or neither;
in this manner, one should declare for the querent the [asterisms] belonging to the wife, siblings, children, and enemies, according to the sign of their rising (*udaya-rāśi*). (Vṛttatilaka)
Years, seasons, months, lunar days, day and night, as well as the stars, times, and the divisions of the ninefold portions of the asterisms— these,
when multiplied by ten and so forth and divided by their own respective denominators, are to be understood through the addition and subtraction of the ninefold units;
likewise, in the case of the decades, the years, seasons, and months are to be known in that same manner.
In the groups of eight as well, the lunar days (tithis) are likewise recorded as half-months.
One should always observe the birth [of phenomena] during day and night, as well as the calculation of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras),
within the groups of seven.
One should understand the *velā*, the *vilagna* (ascendant), the *horā*,
and the *aṃśaka* within the fivefold [calculation] for the purpose of accomplishing the *naṣṭajātaka* (lost-horoscope).
The *saṃskāras*, name, and measure, doubled and joined with the shadow in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), [are used].

The remainder, divided by nine, indicates the lunar mansion starting from Dhaniṣṭhā. (Āryā) Two, three, four, ten, ten, fifteen, seven, three, nine, eight, and eleven; multiplied by five and ten, and added to the respective directions, these are the [values] for the lunar mansions starting from Dhaniṣṭhā. (Āryā)

Thus, this *Naṣṭajāta* of many varieties has been fully expounded by me; it should be accepted by worthy disciples after they have examined it according to its principles. (Āryā E26) [The Nature of the Drekāṇa]
A man with reddened eyes, clad in white garments around his waist like Kṛṣṇa capable of providing protection, bears aloft a fierce axe; (in the Vaitālīya meter:
she who wears red garments, whose thoughts are on ornaments and food, who has the form of a jar, the face of a horse, and is afflicted by thirst.
The Yavanas have taught that the form of the decan (dreṣkāṇa) in the middle of Aries consists of one foot [of the zodiac].
Cruel, skilled in the arts, tawny, seeking wealth, broken in his vows, rising up with an egg in his hand,
wearing red garments, and fierce— this is described as the third third-part (tri-bhāga) in Aries.

With her hair curled and cut short, her body emaciated, wearing burnt garments, and her mind distressed by thirst and hunger, this woman longs for ornaments; such is the form of the first [planet] in the sign of Taurus (Vṛṣabha). [The native] is an expert in agriculture, grain, the household, cattle, and the arts, and is skilled with the plough and the cart.
Bearing a burden like a bull, intent on eating, with a face like a goat and clad in rags—(Svāgatā) With a body like an elephant, white tusks, legs like a śarabha, and a tawny form;
his mind agitated by the desire for sheep and deer, this one has gone to the edge of the bull’s forest. (Dodhaka)
A woman who desires needlework, who is fond of ornaments suited to her form, and who is diligent in her tasks;
one who has few children, raises her arms, and is in her fertile season—those who know [the signs] declare her to be the first third of the third house.
(Va-ti) One situated in a garden, wearing armor, armed with a bow, a hero bearing missiles, and possessing the cry of Garuḍa.
In the middle of the sign of Gemini, one engages in thoughts concerning play, children, ornaments, and wealth.

(Upajātikā) At the end of the sign of Gemini, one is adorned with many jewels like Varuṇa, equipped with a quiver, armor, and a bow, and is learned in the arts of dance and music as well as a composer of poetry. (Svāgatā)

With a body like an elephant carrying leaves, roots, and fruits, dwelling in the Malaya forest, with legs like a śarabha, a face like a boar, and a neck like a horse— this they declare to be the first form in Karkaṭa. (In Svāgatā meter) A woman, adorned with lotuses on her head and joined by a serpent, cries out as she has gone to the forest in Karka.
She rests upon a branch of the *palāśa* tree, situated in the midst of the zodiac sign of Cancer.
A man stands upon a ship in the ocean, encircled by serpents, to obtain ornaments for his wife;
he is adorned with golden decorations, yet possesses a flat face—such is the one who has reached the end [of life] in Cancer.

Above the *śālmali* tree, a vulture, a jackal, a dog, and a man clad in soiled garments cry out, with mother and father interchanged; this is called the first form, that of the lion. A man in the shape of a horse, wearing a crest of white garlands, carries a black antelope skin as a blanket.

Difficult to approach like a lion, with a drawn bow and a nose curved at the tip, he stands in the midst of the lords of beasts; having a bear-like face and the behavior of a monkey, he carries both a staff and fruit as his prey. A man with a beard and curly hair, he is the final third part of the lord of beasts.

A maiden, her body covered with garments stained by impurities, carrying a jar filled with flowers, and desiring the acquisition of clothing and wealth, seeks the family of the Guru; such is the first [result].
(Upajātikā meter) A man, holding a writing brush, dark-complexioned, with prominent veins on his neck, and engaged in physical exercise.
He carries a large bow, his body is covered with hair, and he has a slender waist.

(Vaitālīya) A fair-complexioned woman, veiled in a freshly washed white silk garment, her hands raised toward her hips as if holding a water-pot, proceeds toward the temple of the god with disciplined devotion; they say this indicates that one-third of the [zodiacal] sign is in its final portion. (Upajātikā)
A man standing in the marketplace of another street, carrying a scale and skilled in weights and measures, holds a counterweight in his hand;
he contemplates the merchandise and its price, for the Yavanas say that this is the first form of the scale (tulā).
A man with a vulture-like face, seizing a jar, desires to flee away.

Hungry and thirsty, he thinks in his mind of his wife and children while standing among those who carry scales; adorned with jewels, wearing a golden quiver and armor, that man—who stands in the forest terrifying the deer and assumes the form of a monkey for the sake of fruit and meat—is called a "Yavana" at the end of the scales. (Troṭaka and Vaṃśastha meters)
Deprived of garments and ornaments, a beautiful woman approaches the shore from the great ocean;
fallen from her place, her feet bound by serpents, she is preceded by the sign of Scorpio.
Desiring the pleasures of her former station, the woman’s body is covered by snakes due to the influence of the lunar mansion and the season.
They say its body is like the shell of a tortoise and its middle part has the form of a scorpion.

(Dodhaka meter) With a wide, flattened mouth resembling that of a tortoise, terrifying dogs, deer, boars, and jackals, the lord of beasts protects the region of the Malaya source at the end of the scorpion's [course]. (Puṣpitāgrā meter)
With a body like that of a horse with human-like limbs, standing in the hermitage and holding a long-drawn bow,
he— the first third-part of the bow— protected the ascetics and the materials required for the sacrifice.
(Indravajrā) Beautiful, with a complexion like gold and campaka flowers, she of exquisite form sits upon the auspicious throne.
The middle third of the bow is prescribed as the ocean, churning its jewels.

(Upajātikā) A man with a beard, resembling a golden campaka flower, seated upon an excellent throne and holding a staff, wears silken garments and a deer skin; this is the third form of the ninth zodiac sign. (Upajātikā)
With bristling hair and tusks like those of a makara, his body the size of a boar, wearing a yoke and a net as his bonds, with a fierce face— this was the first makara.
(In *dodhaka* meter) She who is skilled in the arts, with eyes as long as lotus petals, dark-complexioned, and seeking various [ornaments]...
A woman with iron ears adorned with ornaments is assigned to the center of the Makara.

(Upajātikā meter) He who has a body like that of a Kinnara, accompanied by Kambala, and equipped with quivers, bows, and armor—he, the last of the signs in the zodiacal order, carries on his shoulder a water-jar variegated with jewels. (Rathoddhatā meter)
With his mind distracted by the arrival of oil, liquor, water, and food, he carries a blanket;
clothed in a cocoon and clad in skins, with a face like a vulture, he goes about with jars and other vessels.
When the cart and the *śālmali* tree are burnt, he gathers metals in the forest of women.
Covered with a soiled garment and carrying vessels upon his head, he is the Middle One.
Dark-complexioned, with hair reaching his ears and wearing a crown, he carries vessels made of iron mixed with bark, leaves, resin, and fruit;
moving about, he enters into the interior of the jar.
With hands occupied by sacrificial ladles, vessels, pearls, gems, and conch shells, and adorned with ornaments,
he floats upon a boat in the ocean for the sake of decorating his wife, having gone there like a fish; meanwhile,
the ship approaches with its lofty banners and flags, and the retinue proceeds toward the shore of the sea.
A woman with a face like a campaka flower in complexion—this is declared by the sages to be the third part of the Fish, the second [of the zodiacal signs].

(Vaṃśasthavila) Near a chasm, his limbs entwined by a serpent, a man stripped of his garments in the forest, his inner soul agitated by thieves and fire, cries out as he approaches the end of the Fish. (Indravajrā) E27
The divisions of the Upasaṃhāra-rāśi, the distinctions of the planetary origins, birth in non-human wombs, and then the time of conception;
birth, immediate death, as well as lifespan, the ripening of the Daśās, and that which is known as the Aṣṭakavarga. (Upajātikā meter)

Karma, livelihood, royal yoga, sky-yoga, moon-yoga, and yogas such as vigraha; then renunciation, the natures of the signs, aspects, dispositions, the refuge, and finally miscellaneous matters. (In the Śālinī meter:
For women, the desired yogas do not apply to their nativity, nor does the desired birth-decanate lead to their departure [from this world].
Twenty-five chapters have been composed concerning birth; now I shall describe that which pertains to the journey.
(Śālinī meter) The questions, the lunar day, the asterism, the weekday, the hour, the moon, the ascendant, and then the divisions of the ascendant;
the purity of the planets, then the discourse on archery, the section called *Vimiśraka*, and the trembling of the body. (Upajātikā meter)
After this, there shall be the worship of the Guhyakas; then the dream [interpretation], followed by the prescribed rules for bathing.
Then the sacrifice to the planets (graha-yajña), the departure [of the bridegroom], and the instruction on omens (śakuna) are taught in due order.
(Upajātikā meter) The time for marriage and the specific positions of the planets are declared separately; thereafter, the extensive branches [of the science] are explained.
This compendium of astrology consisting of three chapters has been composed by me for the benefit of those who know the divine [sciences].
While this entire treatise was previously composed extensively by others, this work of mine is brief and intended only for the meaning of those specific sections.
Since I am indeed capable here among those whose intellects are like horns, whatever has been said [that is flawed] should be forgiven by virtuous people. (Mālinī meter)

May whatever destruction this work, as it circulates, may suffer through the sequence of being acquired by the mouths of many seekers, or whatever slight error I have committed here, or whatever task remains unaccomplished—may the learned remove that, setting aside all attachment. (Va.Ti.
The son of Ādityadāsa, who has attained awakening and received the grace of a boon from the Sun at Kāpitthaka;
Having thoroughly examined the opinions of the sages of Avanti, Varāhamihira composed this beautiful [work] called the *Vārāhī-saṃhitā*.
By him, whose mind was graced by bowing at the feet of the teacher, the sage Dinakara, this treatise has been compiled. Homage be to the original authors! (Āryā E28)
The End of the Bṛhajjātaka.
